passages.note: House third-reading final passage of SB 101; Soliday is printed in the Yea list and the page carries the tally but not the operative text.

Instrument page for the same record: it establishes that SB 101 is the single-subject bill "Religious freedom restoration" and that it became law, but it prints only a digest, not the operative section.

passages.provision_quote: A person whose exercise of religion has been substantially burdened, or is likely to be substantially burdened, by a violation of this chapter may assert the violation or impending violation as a claim or defense in a judicial or administrative proceeding, regardless of whether the state or any other governmental entity is a party to the proceeding.
passages.note: Enrolled text: Sec. 8 bars a governmental entity from substantially burdening religious exercise "even if the burden results from a rule of general applicability", Sec. 9 (quoted) makes that burden assertable against the law in any proceeding, and Sec. 11 withholds any claim against a private employer.

rows.reasoning: Soliday voted Yea on final passage (third reading, 63-31) of SB 101 (2015), a single-subject bill whose operative chapter bars a governmental entity from substantially burdening a person's exercise of religion "even if the burden results from a rule of general applicability" and lets the person assert that burden "as a claim or defense in a judicial or administrative proceeding" against the law being applied to them; that is the rung that would "protect religious freedom and allow faith-based exemptions from laws that conflict with sincere religious beliefs". The act's own text excludes the rung granting "religious organizations complete autonomy in their operations and hiring practices", because Sec. 11 creates no cause of action against any private employer and Sec. 8(b) still permits a burden that is the least restrictive means of a compelling interest. It also departs from "maintaining equal treatment under the law for all citizens" by exempting religious exercise from laws of general applicability, and the 31 Nay votes put it well clear of near-unanimous.
